learn.hook: The rain that fell on your school today may once have been in the sea, a cloud, or even a leaf! How does water travel?
points: The Sun heats water in seas, rivers, lakes and ponds. The water slowly turns into water vapour and rises. This is evaporation.
High up in the sky, the air is cooler. Water vapour cools and turns into tiny water droplets. This is condensation. Many droplets together form clouds.
When the droplets join and become big and heavy, they fall as rain, snow or hail. This is precipitation.
Rainwater flows into rivers, lakes and seas, and some soaks into the ground. Then the cycle starts again.
Plants also give out water vapour from their leaves. This is called transpiration.

example.q: Meena hangs wet clothes in the sun at 9 a.m. By noon they are dry. Where did the water go?
steps: The Sun warmed the wet clothes.
The water in them turned into water vapour.
The vapour mixed with the air. We cannot see water vapour.
example.answer: The water evaporated into the air as water vapour.

learn.reallife: Drying clothes, a puddle vanishing after rain, and drops on a cold glass of nimbu paani are all parts of the water cycle around you.

options: It happens only once a year

learn.hook: You can live for weeks without food, but only a few days without water. Why is water so special?
points: All living things need water: people, animals and plants.
Water helps us digest food, keeps our body cool and carries waste out of the body. More than half of our body weight is water.
We use water for drinking, cooking, bathing, washing, farming and in factories.
Water covers about three-fourths of the Earth's surface, but most of it is salty sea water. Only a tiny part is fresh water we can use.
We get fresh water from rain, rivers, lakes, ponds, wells and from under the ground (groundwater).

example.q: Our Earth has so much water. Why do people still say there is a shortage of water?
steps: Most of Earth's water is in seas and is salty.
A lot of the fresh water is frozen as ice.
So the water we can drink is only a small part.
example.answer: Because only a very small part of Earth's water is fresh water that we can use.

learn.hook: If every family in your colony saved one bucket of water a day, that would fill a whole tank in a week. Small steps make big savings!
points: We waste water when taps leak, when we leave taps running, or when we let rainwater just flow away.
Rainwater harvesting means collecting rainwater from rooftops and storing it, or sending it into the ground.
Long ago, people in India built stepwells (called baoli or vav), ponds and tanks to store water. Rani ki Vav in Gujarat is a famous stepwell.
In the desert of Rajasthan, people built covered pits called kunds or tankas to collect rainwater. Johads are small earthen dams that hold rainwater.
We can reuse water: water used to wash vegetables or rice can water the plants.

example.q: Aarav brushes his teeth for 2 minutes with the tap running. What can he do to save water?

He can fill a mug and use only that water.
He turns the tap off until he needs to rinse.
example.answer: Use a mug of water and keep the tap closed while brushing.

learn.hook: A river is like a traveller. It is born high in the mountains and walks hundreds of kilometres to meet the sea. Let's follow its path!
points: The place where a river begins is its source. Many Indian rivers begin at a glacier (a huge river of ice) or a spring, high in the mountains.
In the mountains, the river is narrow and flows very fast. It rolls rocks and stones along with it.
In the plains, the river becomes wider and slower. It spreads fine, rich soil called silt on its banks.
Smaller rivers that join a big river are called tributaries. The place where two rivers meet is a confluence (sangam).
The place where a river meets the sea is its mouth. Near the mouth, a river may split into many branches and drop silt to form a delta.

example.q: Why does a river flow fast in the mountains but slowly in the plains?
steps: Water always flows downhill.
In the mountains the slope is steep, so water rushes down.
In the plains the land is almost flat, so water moves slowly.
example.answer: The steep slope of the mountains makes it fast; the flat plains make it slow.

learn.hook: The Ganga begins as icy water from a glacier and ends in a delta with tigers. India's rivers have amazing stories!
points: The Ganga begins at the Gangotri glacier in Uttarakhand. There it is called the Bhagirathi. At Devprayag it joins the Alaknanda and is called the Ganga.
The Yamuna begins at the Yamunotri glacier. It joins the Ganga at Prayagraj. Delhi and Agra are on the banks of the Yamuna.
The Brahmaputra begins in Tibet and flows through Arunachal Pradesh and Assam. Majuli, a huge river island, is in the Brahmaputra.
The Ganga and Brahmaputra flow into the Bay of Bengal and together form the Sundarbans delta, home of the Royal Bengal tiger.
The Narmada begins at Amarkantak in Madhya Pradesh and flows west into the Arabian Sea. The Godavari and Kaveri flow east into the Bay of Bengal.

example.answer: The Yamuna.

Fishermen catch fish, and boats carry people and goods on rivers. Dams on rivers store water and make electricity.
Rivers are home to fish, turtles, crocodiles and the Ganges river dolphin, India's national aquatic animal.
Sewage, factory waste and plastic make rivers dirty. Keeping rivers clean keeps people, animals and plants healthy.

topics.title: The journey of food inside us

learn.hook: You eat a bite of idli. Where does it go next? It takes a long trip through a tube many metres long inside you!
points: Digestion is how our body breaks food down into tiny parts that it can use.
In the mouth, teeth cut and chew food. The tongue mixes it with saliva, which makes it soft and wet.
The food pipe carries food from the mouth to the stomach. In the stomach, digestive juices mix with the food and churn it.
In the small intestine, digestion is completed. The useful parts of food go into the blood and reach every part of the body.
The large intestine takes back water from what is left. The waste then leaves the body.

example.q: Chew a piece of plain roti slowly for a long time. It starts to taste a little sweet. Think it through: why?
steps: Roti has a lot of starch.
Saliva in the mouth starts breaking down starch.
Starch is changed into a kind of sugar, so it tastes sweet.
example.answer: Saliva starts changing the starch in roti into sugar.

learn.reallife: That is why elders say 'chew your food well'. Well-chewed food is easier for the stomach and intestines to digest.

Proteins help us grow and repair the body. Dal, rajma, eggs, fish, milk and paneer give us proteins.
Vitamins and minerals protect us from illness. Fruits, vegetables and milk give us these. Calcium in milk keeps bones and teeth strong.
Roughage (fibre) in fruits, vegetables and whole grains helps food move through the body. Water is also very important.

quiz.mistake: Mixes up protein foods with energy foods

quiz.q: Which nutrient helps the body grow and repair itself?
quiz.explain: Proteins are body-building nutrients. They help us grow and heal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks energy foods build the body

quiz.q: Which mineral in milk keeps bones and teeth strong?
quiz.explain: Calcium makes bones and teeth hard and strong. Milk, curd and ragi have calcium.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up calcium with iron

quiz.q: What does roughage (fibre) do for us?

Makes us taller in one day
quiz.explain: Fibre does not give much energy, but it helps food move smoothly through the intestines.
quiz.mistake: Thinks fibre has no use because it is not digested

quiz.q: Which fruit is very rich in vitamin C?
quiz.explain: Amla (Indian gooseberry) has a lot of vitamin C, which helps keep gums and skin healthy.
quiz.mistake: Picks a fruit known for energy rather than vitamin C

quiz.q: Our body can make vitamin D when our skin gets
quiz.explain: When sunlight falls on our skin, the body makes vitamin D, which helps keep bones strong.
quiz.mistake: Does not know sunlight helps make vitamin D

quiz.q: Which of these foods is rich in fats?
quiz.explain: Butter, ghee, oil and nuts are rich in fats, which also give energy.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up fat-rich foods with fruits and vegetables

teach.ask: Gappu pecks at a plate: 'Why can't I just eat sweets all day? What do different foods do?'
teach.praise: Oh! Some foods give energy, some help me grow and some protect me. Sweets alone can't do all that!
teach.nudge: Which foods help us grow? And which foods protect us from falling ill?

topics.title: Balanced diet and healthy food habits

learn.hook: Eating only aloo paratha every day sounds yummy, but your body would miss many things. What does a happy, healthy plate look like?
points: A balanced diet has all the nutrients in the right amounts, along with water and roughage.
Millets like ragi, bajra and jowar are healthy grains grown in India. The year 2023 was celebrated as the International Year of Millets.
Junk food has too much oil, salt or sugar and few useful nutrients. We should eat it only once in a while.
Wash your hands before eating, wash fruits and vegetables, and keep food covered.
Food can be kept from spoiling by keeping it cool, drying it (like papad) or using salt, oil or sugar (like pickles and jam).

example.q: Riya's lunch is two samosas and a cold drink. Think it through: is it a balanced meal? How can she improve it?
steps: Samosas are fried, so they have a lot of fat and carbohydrates.
The cold drink has a lot of sugar.
There is little protein, vitamins or fibre.
She can eat roti with dal, sabzi, salad and a glass of buttermilk instead.
example.answer: It is not balanced. A meal like roti, dal, sabzi, salad and buttermilk is better.

learn.reallife: Many government schools serve hot cooked mid-day meals (the PM POSHAN scheme). These meals include grains, dal and vegetables to keep children healthy.

Food eaten while standing on one leg

quiz.q: Why should we eat junk food only once in a while?

quiz.q: Which is a sign that food has gone bad?
options: It is on a clean plate
It smells bad or has fuzzy mould on it
quiz.explain: A bad smell, a strange taste or mould means germs have spoilt the food.
quiz.mistake: Does not know the signs of spoilt food

teach.ask: Gappu holds a jalebi: 'If jalebis taste so good, why can't I eat only jalebis? What is a balanced diet?'
teach.praise: I get it! A little of everything in the right amounts, and jalebis only sometimes. My tummy says thank you!
teach.nudge: What should a healthy plate have? And why is too much junk food a problem?

learn.hook: Who opens the school gate before you arrive? Who makes the garden bloom? A school runs because many people work together!
points: A school community is all the people who make the school work: students, teachers, the principal, office staff, cleaning staff, the gardener, the guard, cooks and bus drivers.
Each person's work is important, so we respect and thank everyone.
Parents also help. They meet teachers and may be part of the School Management Committee.
Students help too: as class monitors, in the eco-club, by keeping the classroom clean and caring for the school garden.
A good school welcomes everyone. Ramps help wheelchair users, books in Braille help children who cannot see, and sign language helps children who cannot hear.

example.q: A new girl, Lhamo, uses a wheelchair. Her classroom is on the first floor and there is no ramp or lift. Think it through: what can the school do?
steps: Every child has the right to reach the classroom.
A ramp or lift would help her move on her own.
Until then, the class could be moved to the ground floor.
example.answer: Build a ramp or lift, and meanwhile hold her class on the ground floor.

learn.reallife: Next time you see the school guard, the cleaning didi or bhaiya, or the gardener, say 'Thank you!' They help make your school a happy place.

pairs: Cares for plants in the school garden

options: Students, teachers, staff and parents together
Only the people who live near the school
quiz.explain: Everyone who helps the school run is part of its community.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only teachers or students make a school

quiz.q: Who usually looks after the plants in the school garden?
quiz.explain: The gardener (mali) waters, plants and cares for the school garden.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up the jobs of school staff

quiz.q: Why should we respect the cleaning staff of our school?
options: They are the oldest people in school
Their work keeps the school clean and healthy for all
quiz.explain: Every job in school is important. A clean school keeps all of us healthy.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only some jobs deserve respect

quiz.q: Braille is a way of reading using
options: raised dots felt with the fingers
quiz.explain: Braille uses patterns of raised dots. People who cannot see read them with their fingertips.
quiz.mistake: Does not know how Braille works

quiz.q: Who invented Braille?
quiz.explain: Louis Braille of France made this reading system. He had lost his own eyesight as a child.

quiz.q: What helps a child who uses a wheelchair enter the school building on their own?
quiz.explain: A ramp is a gentle slope, so a wheelchair can roll up it.
quiz.mistake: Does not think about how wheelchairs move

quiz.q: How can students help keep their school a happy place?
options: Keep classrooms clean and be kind to everyone
quiz.explain: Clean, cared-for classrooms and kind friends make school pleasant for all.

quiz.q: The School Management Committee includes
quiz.explain: Parents, teachers and local members meet to help plan and improve the school.
quiz.mistake: Does not know parents help run schools

teach.ask: Gappu lands on the school gate: 'Is a school just teachers and children? Who else makes it work?'
teach.praise: So many helpers! Teachers, students, staff and parents all work together. I respect them all now!
teach.nudge: Who else, besides teachers and students, works to keep a school running?

learn.hook: Have you ever felt happy, nervous and excited all on the same day? Feelings are normal, and a happy school helps everyone feel safe.
points: Everyone has feelings: happy, sad, angry, scared or excited. All feelings are okay. Talking about them helps.
When we feel upset, we can take deep breaths, count to ten, or talk to a friend, parent or teacher.
Being kind means sharing, helping, listening and including others in games.
Bullying means hurting someone again and again with words or actions. It is never okay. Tell a teacher or a trusted adult.
Our body is our own. If any touch makes you feel uncomfortable, say 'No', move away, and tell a trusted adult.

example.q: At lunch, Samar sees some children laughing at a new boy's accent every day. Think it through: what should Samar do?
steps: Laughing at someone again and again is bullying.
Samar can be kind to the new boy and sit with him.
He should tell the class teacher so that the bullying stops.
example.answer: Be kind to the new boy and tell a teacher about the bullying.

learn.reallife: Many schools start the day with yoga or a few minutes of quiet breathing. It helps both the body and the mind feel fresh.

quiz.explain: Slow breathing helps the body relax so we can think clearly.

quiz.q: What is bullying?
options: Hurting someone again and again with words or actions
quiz.explain: Bullying is repeated hurting, teasing or leaving someone out on purpose.
quiz.mistake: Thinks only hitting counts as bullying

quiz.explain: A trusted adult can help stop the bullying. You do not have to handle it alone.

quiz.explain: A trusted adult is someone who cares for you, like a parent, grandparent or teacher.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any grown-up can be trusted

quiz.q: Which of these helps keep our body and mind healthy?
options: Sitting with a phone all night
Playing, enough sleep and healthy food
quiz.explain: Exercise, sleep and good food keep us fit, fresh and in a good mood.

options: Talking to her teacher and taking deep breaths
quiz.explain: Sharing the feeling and breathing slowly can calm nervousness. Feeling nervous is normal.
quiz.mistake: Thinks nervous feelings should be hidden

options: It's okay, everyone makes mistakes. Let's try again.
quiz.explain: Kind words help a friend feel better and try again.
quiz.mistake: Thinks making fun of mistakes is harmless

teach.ask: Gappu looks sad: 'A big bird laughs at my small wings every day. What should I do? How do we make school happy?'
teach.praise: Thank you! Being laughed at again and again is bullying, so I will tell my teacher. And I'll be kind to others too.
teach.nudge: What can I do if someone keeps hurting me? Who can I tell?

learn.hook: Fire drills, earthquake drills, first aid boxes: schools practise safety so that everyone knows what to do if something goes wrong.
points: In an earthquake: Drop to the floor, take Cover under a strong desk, and Hold on until the shaking stops.
During a fire drill: stay calm, walk quickly in a line, do not run or push, use the stairs (never the lift), and go to the safe open ground.
For a small cut: wash it with clean water, cover it with a clean bandage, and tell an adult.
On the road: cross at a zebra crossing. Look right, then left, then right again. Red light means stop and green light means go.
In India, 112 is the one number to call for police, fire or ambulance help in an emergency.

example.q: The fire alarm rings during class. Two children want to run to the lift to get out quickly. Think it through: what should the class do?
steps: Lifts can stop working in a fire and trap people.
Running and pushing can make people fall.
So the class should line up, walk quickly down the stairs and go to the open ground.
example.answer: Walk calmly in a line, use the stairs, not the lift, and gather in the open ground.

learn.reallife: Find your school's first aid box and the fire extinguisher. Do you know where the assembly point is during a drill?

quiz.explain: Fire can cut the electricity, so a lift may get stuck. Stairs are safer.
quiz.mistake: Does not know lifts can fail in a fire

quiz.q: Which is the right way to cross a road?
options: Cross while looking at a phone
At the zebra crossing, after looking right, left and right again
Cross from behind a parked bus
quiz.explain: Zebra crossings are made for walkers, and looking both ways makes sure no vehicle is coming.
quiz.mistake: Does not know safe road-crossing rules

quiz.q: Which number can you call in India for police, fire or ambulance help?
quiz.explain: 112 is India's single emergency number for all urgent help.
quiz.mistake: Guesses a number from films or other countries

quiz.q: Aditi gets a small scrape on her knee while playing. What should be done first?
options: Wash it with clean water and cover it with a clean bandage
Ignore it and keep it dirty
Rub it with a dirty cloth
quiz.explain: Clean water washes away dirt and germs, and a bandage keeps the wound clean.
quiz.mistake: Thinks home remedies like mud are safe for wounds

quiz.q: What does a yellow (amber) traffic light usually tell drivers?
quiz.explain: Amber means the light is about to change, so drivers should slow down and get ready to stop.
quiz.mistake: Thinks amber means hurry up

quiz.q: Why does a school hold fire drills and earthquake drills?
options: So everyone knows what to do and stays calm in a real emergency
quiz.explain: Practice helps us act quickly and safely without panic.
quiz.mistake: Does not see the point of practice

quiz.q: During a fire drill, the class should

go back for their bags and toys

teach.ask: Gappu hears a loud bell: 'Ring ring! Is that a fire drill? What do I do?'
teach.praise: Got it! Stay calm, walk in a line, take the stairs and wait in the open ground. I'm a drill expert now!
teach.nudge: Should I run or walk? And should I take the lift or the stairs?

learn.hook: In one train journey across India, you could hear ten languages, taste twenty kinds of rotis and see snow, deserts and beaches. Yet we are all Indians!
points: India has 28 states and 8 union territories. New Delhi is the capital of India.
People in India speak many languages. The Constitution lists 22 languages in its Eighth Schedule, including Hindi, Tamil, Bengali, Marathi and Assamese.
India has snowy mountains, hot deserts, green forests, long coasts and wide plains. So people's food, clothes and homes are different in different places.
People of many faiths live together and enjoy one another's festivals.
We celebrate national festivals together: Republic Day (26 January), Independence Day (15 August) and Gandhi Jayanti (2 October).

example.q: People in Ladakh wear thick woollen clothes, while people in Kerala wear light cotton. Think it through: why?
steps: Ladakh is high in the mountains and is very cold.
Kerala is near the sea and is warm and humid.
People choose clothes that suit the weather of their place.
example.answer: Because the weather is different: cold in Ladakh, warm in Kerala.

learn.reallife: Look at a ₹10 note. Its value is written in many Indian languages: a small sign of our unity in diversity.

teach.ask: Gappu flies over a map: 'Why does India have so many languages, foods and clothes? Is it still one country?'

learn.hook: Bihu in Assam, Onam in Kerala, Pongal in Tamil Nadu: every state has its own festivals, dances and tasty food. Let's go on a culture trip!
points: Many festivals are linked to harvests: Pongal in Tamil Nadu, Bihu in Assam, Onam in Kerala and Baisakhi in Punjab.
Each state has its own dances: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathakali (Kerala), Bhangra (Punjab), Garba (Gujarat), Ghoomar (Rajasthan) and Odissi (Odisha).
Each region has special food: dhokla from Gujarat, litti chokha from Bihar, dal baati churma from Rajasthan, and makki di roti with sarson da saag from Punjab.
The Hornbill Festival of Nagaland shows the dances, songs and crafts of the state's many tribes.
Every state has a capital. For example, Dispur is the capital of Assam and Jaipur is the capital of Rajasthan.

example.q: Neha's family is going to see the boat races during Onam. Which state will they visit?
steps: Onam is the harvest festival of Kerala.
Snake-boat races are held on Kerala's backwaters around Onam.
So they will visit Kerala.
example.answer: Kerala.

learn.reallife: Next time you eat at a wedding or a food fair, try a dish from another state and find out where it comes from!

teach.nudge: Can you tell me where Bihu or Garba come from? What else is special about each state?

learn.hook: Fish and peacocks painted in Bihar, stick-figure dancers painted in Maharashtra: Indian art tells stories in many styles!
points: Madhubani paintings come from Bihar. They use bright colours and pictures of fish, birds and nature.
Warli paintings come from Maharashtra. They use white stick figures of people, animals and trees.
Gond paintings come from Madhya Pradesh and are made with lines and dots. Blue pottery is a famous craft of Jaipur in Rajasthan.

The banyan is our national tree and the mango is our national fruit.

steps: Madhubani uses bright colours and fish and bird designs.
Warli uses simple white stick figures.
So the painting is Warli art.
example.answer: Warli art from Maharashtra.

learn.reallife: Look around at a craft fair or museum: you may spot Madhubani, Warli or blue pottery. Each tells the story of the place where it was made.

learn.hook: Some deserts burn hot with golden sand. Others are freezing cold with snowy mountains! India has both kinds.
points: A desert is a place that gets very little rain.
The Thar Desert is a hot desert, mostly in Rajasthan. It has sand dunes, very hot days and cool nights. Jaisalmer is a city in the Thar.
Ladakh is a cold desert. It is high in the mountains, gets very little rain, and has freezing winters.
The camel is called the 'ship of the desert'. Its wide, padded feet do not sink in sand, and its hump stores fat, not water. In Ladakh's Nubra Valley there are two-humped camels.
The Rann of Kutch in Gujarat is a huge salt desert. In winter it shines white like snow.

example.q: Think it through: why do houses in the Thar Desert often have thick mud walls?
steps: Days in the desert are very hot.
Thick mud walls do not let heat in quickly.
So the inside of the house stays cooler during the day.
example.answer: Thick mud walls keep the house cool in the hot desert.

learn.hook: Bridges made of living tree roots, a lake with floating islands, and the tallest mountains on Earth: India's wonders are real!
points: The Himalayas in the north are the highest mountains in the world. Mount Everest, the world's highest peak, stands on the border of Nepal and China.
Kangchenjunga, on the border of Sikkim and Nepal, is the third-highest peak in the world. You can see it from Sikkim and Darjeeling.
In hills, houses often have sloping roofs so that rain and snow slide off easily.
Mawsynram and Sohra (Cherrapunji) in Meghalaya are among the wettest places on Earth. People there grow living root bridges from the roots of rubber fig trees.

topics.title: Forms of energy and how they change

learn.hook: A fan spins, a bulb glows, a pressure cooker whistles and you run around the playground. All of this needs energy!
points: Energy is what makes things work, move, grow, light up or heat up.
Energy comes in many forms: heat, light, sound, electrical energy and the energy of moving things.
Energy can be stored. Food, fuels like LPG and wood, and batteries all hold stored (chemical) energy.
Energy changes from one form to another. A fan changes electrical energy into movement. A bulb changes electrical energy into light and some heat.
Our body changes the stored energy of food into movement and body heat.

Non-renewable sources will run out one day: coal, petroleum (from which petrol and diesel are made) and natural gas. They formed deep underground over millions of years.

Biogas is made from cow dung and kitchen waste. Dams use flowing water to make electricity.

learn.hook: Your cotton T-shirt grew on a plant, your woollen sweater was once on a sheep, and your raincoat came from petroleum! Clothes have surprising beginnings.
points: Clothes are made of fabric, and fabric is made of thin threads called fibres.
Plant fibres: cotton comes from the fluffy balls (bolls) of the cotton plant, jute from the stem of the jute plant, and coir from coconut husks.
Animal fibres: wool comes from the hair of sheep, goats, yaks and camels. Silk comes from the cocoons made by silkworms.
Synthetic (man-made) fibres like nylon and polyester are made in factories from chemicals that come from petroleum.
Cotton soaks up sweat and is cool for summer. Wool traps air and keeps us warm in winter.

example.q: Think it through: why is cotton better than nylon for a hot summer day in Chennai?
steps: In hot weather we sweat a lot.
Cotton soaks up sweat and lets air pass through.
Nylon does not soak up sweat well, so we feel sticky.

learn.hook: A cotton ball and a shirt look nothing alike. How does fluffy cotton become a smart school shirt? Let's follow the steps!
points: Cotton bolls are picked from the plants. Then the seeds are removed from the cotton. This is called ginning.
Fibres are twisted together to make a long thread called yarn. This is spinning. A charkha (spinning wheel) or a takli can spin yarn by hand.
Yarn is woven or knitted into fabric. Fabric is dyed or printed in colours, then cut and stitched into clothes.
For wool, sheep's hair is cut off (shearing, which does not hurt the sheep, like a haircut). It is washed, sorted, combed and spun into yarn.
For silk, silkworms spin cocoons. The fine silk thread is unwound from the cocoons and woven into silk fabric.

example.q: Mahatma Gandhi spun yarn on a charkha every day. Think it through: what is khadi?
steps: Gandhiji wanted Indians to make their own cloth.
Yarn was spun by hand on a charkha.
The yarn was then woven by hand into cloth.
example.answer: Khadi is cloth made from hand-spun and hand-woven yarn.

points: Weaving uses two sets of threads crossing each other at right angles on a loom. The long threads are the warp and the threads going across are the weft.

Famous textiles: Banarasi silk from Varanasi, Kanchipuram silk from Tamil Nadu, Pochampally ikat from Telangana, golden Muga silk from Assam, and Bandhani tie-dye from Gujarat and Rajasthan.

learn.hook: Right now, while you are reading this, the ground under you is spinning! That spinning gives us day and night.
points: The Earth is shaped like a ball (a sphere). It spins on an imaginary line called its axis. This spinning is called rotation.
The Earth takes about 24 hours to spin once. That makes one day and one night.
The half of the Earth facing the Sun has day. The half facing away from the Sun has night.
Because the Earth spins from west to east, the Sun seems to rise in the east and set in the west.
Shadows are long in the morning and evening, and shortest around noon when the Sun is high in the sky.

steps: The torch is like the Sun.

As the globe turns, places move from light to dark: day changes to night.
example.answer: The spinning Earth gives day to the side facing the Sun and night to the other side.

learn.hook: Mangoes in summer, rain in the monsoon, warm sweaters in winter: nature repeats its patterns every year like a song with a beat!
points: The Earth goes around the Sun. This is called revolution. One trip takes about 365 days, which is one year.
The Earth's axis is tilted. Because of this tilt, different places get different amounts of sunlight during the year, and we get seasons.
In India we have summer, the monsoon (rainy season), autumn, winter and spring. Traditional Indian calendars name six seasons, called ritus.
The Moon seems to change shape. From one new moon (amavasya) to the next full moon (purnima) takes about 15 days, and the whole cycle takes about a month.
Plants follow cycles too. Many trees shed leaves and grow new ones every year. The Neelakurinji flower of the Western Ghats blooms only once in 12 years!

example.q: A year usually has 365 days, but almost every fourth year has 366 days. Think it through: why?
steps: The Earth takes about 365 and a quarter days to go around the Sun.
Four quarters add up to one whole day.
So every four years, one extra day (29 February) is added.
example.answer: To add up the extra quarter days; that year is a leap year.

learn.reallife: Many Indian festivals follow nature's rhythm: Diwali falls on a new moon night, Holi near a full moon, and harvest festivals in spring and winter.

learn.hook: Every winter, thousands of birds fly over the Himalayas to visit India, and some come all the way from Central Asia and Siberia. Why do they make such long trips?
points: Migration is when animals travel far from one place to another at a certain time of the year, and later return.
Animals migrate to find food, to escape the cold, or to lay eggs and raise their young.
Amur falcons stop in Nagaland every October–November on their long journey to Africa. Bar-headed geese fly over the Himalayas to spend the winter in India.
Flamingos raise their chicks in the Rann of Kutch. Demoiselle cranes spend winter in Khichan village, Rajasthan.

Olive Ridley sea turtles come in huge numbers to lay eggs on Odisha's beaches. Some herders, like the Gaddis of Himachal Pradesh, move with their flocks to the hills in summer and back down in winter.

example.q: In winter, many lakes in Siberia freeze over. Think it through: why do some birds from there fly to India in winter?
steps: Frozen lakes mean birds cannot find fish, insects or plants to eat.
India is warmer in winter, and its lakes and wetlands have food.
So the birds fly to India for the winter and go back in spring.
example.answer: They come to find food and warmth, and go back when the cold ends.

learn.hook: A banana peel can turn into soil in a few weeks, but a plastic bottle can stay around for hundreds of years. What happens to the things we throw away?
points: Pollution means making air, water or land dirty and harmful.
Smoke from vehicles, factories and burning garbage pollutes the air. Sewage and waste pollute water. Plastic and garbage pollute land.
Follow the 3 Rs: Reduce (use less), Reuse (use again) and Recycle (make new things from old ones).
Separate waste at home: wet waste like peels and leftover food goes in the green bin; dry waste like paper, plastic, metal and glass goes in the blue bin.
Wet kitchen waste can be turned into compost, a natural manure for plants. Carry a cloth bag instead of taking plastic bags.

example.q: After a birthday party, there are banana peels, paper plates, plastic spoons and a glass bottle. Think it through: how should they be sorted?

Paper plates, plastic spoons and the glass bottle are dry waste for the blue bin.

learn.hook: Have you heard grown-ups say 'summers are getting hotter'? Scientists have found that the Earth is slowly warming. What can we do about it?
points: Weather is what the sky and air are like today: sunny, rainy or windy. Climate is the usual weather of a place over many years.
Burning coal, petrol and diesel, and cutting down forests, add a lot of carbon dioxide to the air. This gas traps heat, so the Earth is slowly getting warmer.
A warmer Earth means melting glaciers, rising sea levels, more heatwaves, and very heavy rain or long dry spells in some places.
Trees take in carbon dioxide and give out oxygen. Forests also give homes to animals and keep the soil in place.
We can help: plant and care for trees, save electricity, walk, cycle or use buses, and waste less.

example.q: Mumbai is warm and humid all year, while Shimla is cool most of the year. Is this weather or climate? Think it through.

example.answer: It is climate: the usual weather of a place over many years.

learn.hook: Ordinary people in India have hugged trees, grown whole forests and protected animals. You can be an Earth hero too!

The Bishnoi people of Rajasthan have protected trees and animals like blackbucks for hundreds of years. In 1730, Amrita Devi and many villagers bravely stood up to save khejri trees.
